subject: research/robofab-edgeconv
professional: a robotics researcher in time-optimal path parameterisation and trajectory planning (TOPP, Bobrow/Pfeiffer/Verscheure/Pham lineage) refereeing for ICRA/RA-L or a motion-planning workshop; they would check first that the solver's convergence claim is shown on the quantity that matters, that the comparator (trapezoid) is itself converged, and that the 'edge' is not an artefact of a constraint that dominates both profiles

evidence.correctness: Ran the full experiment in a scratch copy (`PYTHONPATH=src python3 experiments/run.py`, about 3 min): all 12 rows byte-identical to experiments/results.txt (diff SAME). Recomputed independently (scripts outside the repo): (1) the arm.torque dynamics against a from-scratch Lagrangian (energy functions, finite-difference Euler-Lagrange) at 20 random states: max difference 4e-7 N m, so the physics is right. (2) Arithmetic of results.json: T_ext = T6400-(T1600-T6400)/3 and edge_6400 = 1-T/T_trap reproduce for all 12 rows to 1e-6; the README ranges (solver moves 0.006 to 0.463 percent from 400 to 6400; step ratios 4.1 to 84.9; 7 negative edges at n=400, 5 of them at 1 rad/s) are all right. (3) Closed-form lower bound for the 1 rad/s rows (0.12 m, no jaw cap): with wmax binding the minimum time is sum(max|dq|)/wmax = 10.111 s; the solver gives 10.115 at n=6400 (0.04 percent above, as an Euler scheme should be), and an independent re-evaluation of the solved profile's torque with the Lagrangian peaks at 0.5 to 1.8 N m against the 5 N m limit, so at 1 rad/s the torque limit is nowhere near active. (4) Because the speed cap dominates, the trapezoid time is approximately LB/(1-f). The best ramp fraction chosen for ALL six parts at 0.12 m, 1 rad/s is 0.002, the smallest value on the grid (run.py:10). Re-running trap.best_trap with 0.0005 and 0.001 added (same code, ramp_samples=40) gives 0.0005 or 0.001 for every part and a trapezoid total of 10.117 s instead of 10.132, i.e. the edge over the n=6400 solver falls from +0.17 percent to +0.02 percent, within the solver's own 0.04 percent overshoot over the lower bound. So the headline 'positive in all 12 rows' is not established for the speed-limited rows: it is the comparator grid, not the planner, that gives the positive sign. Torque physics and the solver's convergence numbers are correct; the headline inference is not.
evidence.completeness: README claims checked: 12 rows x 6 parts all feasible (yes, parts=6 in every row); three node counts per row (yes); Richardson column (yes); 47 tests (yes, 47 OK); `<10 s` tests (5 s); 'about 2 min' experiment (about 3 min here, close); results.json and edge.svg and figure.py exist (figure content not inspected); live page URL not loaded. No stubs or TODOs. Stated out-of-scope items (finer trapezoid grid, unlimited-speed rows, absolute jerk, MuJoCo) are listed as Next steps. The finer-trapezoid-grid item is exactly the one that decides the headline, so the project is finished as scoped but its own first next step is the missing piece.
evidence.verification: `PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m unittest discover -s tests`: 47 tests, OK in 5 s. Mutation 1 (topp.py:129, forward acceleration inflated by 5 percent): 2 failures. Mutation 2 (trap.py min_time_trap, speed-limit check loosened by 20 percent): 2 failures. Both reverted with git checkout; git status clean for research/robofab-edgeconv. Good catching power for core arithmetic, mostly inherited from parent projects (closed-form single-joint bang-bang test, inverse-sqrt-torque scaling test). Weaknesses: the one new test (test_time_converges_with_node_count) only asserts monotone shrinking steps, so it would pass if the comparator or the Richardson step were wrong; nothing tests that the chosen ramp fraction is interior to the grid, or the run.py aggregation.
evidence.craft: Read topp.py, trap.py, model.py (head), run.py and the tests. Readable, stdlib-only, docstrings explain physics, and sources (Bobrow, Pfeiffer) are named. Defects: (a) the five modules are a copy of robofab-scurvefine (the README says so), so an engine exists in at least 6 projects, any fix must be repeated; (b) topp.py:163 re-imports G locally though it is imported at line 13; (c) no input validation in solve (qa==qb, tau<=0, wmax<=0, n<2) and infeasibility returns None with no reason; (d) run.py silently `continue`s past an infeasible part or row (lines 26-35) so a skipped part would shrink the six-part total, protected only by the printed parts column; (e) run.py is a module-level script with the hard-coded path 'experiments/results.json' and a result json.dump without closing the file; (f) the forward pass is explicit Euler (topp.py:129) with acceleration taken at the node, so constraints are only met to O(ds), and the test allows 3 percent torque violation; (g) the Richardson step is applied although the data show a ratio of 4 to 85, flagged by the README but still printed as a column.
evidence.claims: Backed by files: all of the numeric claims of the first, second and third bullets are reproducible from results.txt/json (recomputed above), the 'solver totals agree with solver_n.txt' claim, 47 tests, MIT, standard library only, 'not endorsed by' disclaimer, 'Stylised' label. Not backed or overstated: (a) 'the time-optimal edge ... is positive in all 12 rows' and 'the negatives ... were the solver's discretisation' (README:8) hold only against a trapezoid whose best ramp fraction sits at the grid edge in the 1 rad/s rows; with two finer values the edge in the 0.12 m, 1 rad/s, no-cap row is +0.02 percent (see correctness); the limitation is acknowledged ('a finer grid could shave the edge further') but the headline and Reading bullet are stated unqualified and the title question is answered 'yes'. (b) 'solver side is now converged to a few hundredths of a percent' is estimated from three nodes counts, not bounded. (c) 'a well-tuned trapezoid' is not what the grid-limited comparator is. (d) No statement that at 1 rad/s the torque limit is inactive (peak 0.5 to 1.8 of 5 N m) so the 'edge' there is a pure ramp-duration effect, not a torque-optimality effect; that is what a reader needs to interpret the number. (e) No novelty position and no prior-work citations beyond the parent projects. Disclaimer and Stylised label are present.
evidence.fitness: Could a researcher build on it? Partly. As an internal calibration note it does its job: it shows that a 400-node explicit-Euler TOPP undershoots by up to 0.46 percent, which is useful if one reuses the sibling projects. As research it is a numerical-convergence check on a toy (two links, fixed joint-space line, round-number parameters, no motors) whose result is the opposite of surprising (a finer grid shrinks a discretisation error). Nearest prior work: the TOPP literature (Bobrow, Dubowsky, Gibson 1985; Pfeiffer and Johanni 1987; Shiller; Verscheure et al. 2009 on convex-optimal TOPP, which has no node-count error; Pham and Pham 2014 TOPP-RA with exact-per-segment guarantees), plus standard jerk-limited trajectory work (Kroger, Ruckig). A TOPP referee would ask why an explicit-Euler scheme is used rather than the exact piecewise formulation, and would regard the 0.1 to 0.9 percent 'edge' as something that disappears when the trapezoid's ramp is tuned continuously (the f->0 limit is the speed-limited bound). None is cited. Not part of a programme in PROGRAMMES.md, so well below the PhD+ aim in research/CLAUDE.md. The finding most useful to later projects (robofab-cell, selfrep) is the unwritten one: at 1 rad/s the speed limit, not torque, sets the time, so planner choice barely matters.
evidence.domain: Compared against TOPP practice and industrial trajectory generation. A senior planner would accept the forward-backward integration with a velocity limit curve and the Lagrangian dynamics (verified). Departures: explicit Euler over u=s'^2 with per-node acceleration bounds rather than an exact or convex formulation, so constraints are met only to O(ds); convergence judged on a six-part sum rather than per-part; a trapezoid comparator tuned on a 14-point grid when the optimum is at its edge (a one-dimensional continuous search is trivial); the 'edge' quoted in percent of a six-part sum without a note that the lower bound sum(dq)/wmax is within 0.04 percent of both profiles at 1 rad/s; no motor/drive model, no jerk limit in absolute units, no joint-space path optimisation (the line is fixed), so the comparison is between two time-scalings of one path. A practitioner would not read 'time-optimal beats a tuned trapezoid by 0.2 percent' as a design input.

defects.what: The comparator's best ramp fraction is the grid minimum (0.002) for every part in the speed-limited rows checked; adding 0.0005 and 0.001 reduces the 0.12 m, 1 rad/s, no-cap edge from +0.17 to +0.02 percent (within the solver's 0.04 percent overshoot over the sum(dq)/wmax lower bound). The headline 'positive in all 12 rows' and 'the negatives were the discretisation' are therefore not established.

README states the edge result and the Reading bullet unqualified; the grid caveat sits only in Limitations, and it never says the torque limit is inactive at 1 rad/s (peak 0.5 to 1.8 of 5 N m), where the 'edge' is just ramp duration.

New test only checks that solver steps shrink; nothing tests the comparator is converged (best fraction interior to the grid) or that Richardson/edge arithmetic in run.py is right, so the central weakness above cannot be caught by the suite.
Solver engine copied across robofab-* projects; local redundant re-import of G; no input validation, None returned without a reason; run.py silently skips infeasible parts.
Explicit-Euler forward/backward pass uses node-k acceleration bounds, so constraints hold only to O(ds); Richardson column printed although step ratios range 4 to 85.
No prior-work positioning (TOPP-RA, convex TOPP, Ruckig) and no programme membership in PROGRAMMES.md.

verdict: A tidy, reproducible, stdlib-only follow-up: 47 tests pass, the full experiment reproduces results.txt exactly, the dynamics match an independent Lagrangian to 4e-7 N m, the solver's node-count numbers and their arithmetic are right, and two seeded mutations were caught. It does not meet the bar because the headline conclusion is not sound as stated: in the 1 rad/s rows the speed limit alone sets the time (torque is far from binding), the solver is within 0.04 percent of the closed-form lower bound sum(dq)/wmax, and the trapezoid it is compared with has its best ramp fraction pinned at the smallest grid value; two finer values cut the edge from +0.17 to +0.02 percent in a row I re-ran, so 'positive in all 12 rows' is an artefact of the comparator grid, which the README's own first Next step would have caught. Scores: correctness 2 (physics and arithmetic right, headline inference not), claims 2, craft 2, fitness 2 and domain 2 (a discretisation-convergence note on a toy, no novelty position, not in a programme), completeness 3 and verification 3. Cheapest fix: replace the 14-point grid by a continuous 1-D search (or add f below 0.002), re-run, and restate the edge, probably as 'not distinguishable from zero at 1 rad/s'.
